script.title: Why ₹10 Snacks Keep Getting Smaller #shorts

segments.text: Your ten-rupee snack packet is not full of air by accident.
segments.broll: person opening snack bag close up

segments.text: In India, brands know you will stop buying if the price jumps to eleven rupees.
That single extra coin breaks our hardwired mental budget.
segments.broll: hand holding five rupee coin macro

segments.text: So instead of raising the price tag, companies secretly slash the packet weight.
This sneaky trick is shrinkflation, and it hits your biscuits, namkeen, and soaps.
You still hand over a ten-rupee coin, but get twenty percent less food inside.
segments.broll: digital kitchen scale weighing close up

segments.text: You feel like inflation spared you, until you wonder why...

script.loop_line: You feel like inflation spared you, until you wonder why...
script.description: Ever wonder why your favorite biscuit or chips packet feels lighter even though you still pay ₹10? FMCG brands use a pricing trick called shrinkflation to protect their margins without scaring buyers away. Here is the hidden retail economics behind magic price points in India. #BusinessStrategy #IndianEconomy #PaisaDecoded

facts_to_verify.claim: FMCG brands in India maintain fixed price points (₹5, ₹10) and reduce packet weight (shrinkflation) instead of raising headline prices.
Shrinkflation affects fast-moving consumer goods like biscuits, snacks, and soaps.

script.chosen_candidate: Shrinkflation: Why the RBI Rate Hike May Fail in 2026 - Frontline Magazine
script.why_it_will_work: Every young Indian buys ₹5 and ₹10 packaged snacks daily, making this silent FMCG pricing tactic instantly relatable, debate-worthy, and visual.
